newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee, oil top commodity rally, funds busy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee, oil top commodity rally, funds busy.

text.p: Speculative buying reignited this year's rally in world coffee prices on Monday and buying by funds also helped lift crude oil and metals markets.
Gold firmed, helped by a weak dollar, but wheat bucked the trend and slipped quite sharply.
Coffee futures shot up at midsession in New York, with the July contract setting a new contract high, bolstered by trade and speculative buying against a background of supply concerns, dealers said.
July reached 228.25 cents per lb, up 10.35 cents on the day.
Traders said sentiment was buoyed by a report from brokerage Merrill Lynch, which said coffee prices could reach record highs ahead of new crop shipments this autumn, because supply is tight.
Arabica coffee prices have more than doubled this year and values for the less-prized robustas, traded in London, are up by about one-third.
Crude oil prices also rose sharply on Monday.
North Sea Brent Blend crude oil, the world benchmark, rose sharply in London's afternoon on the back of technical fund-led buying after a strong opening in New York oil futures.
The June Brent contract reached a high of $19.60 which was 60 cents up on the open.
Tension caused by the start of Iranian wargames in the Gulf on Sunday and a consequent U.S. pledge to defend the area against any threat added support to crude prices.
"All this tension helps, doesn't it? But mainly it is generally technical," one oil trader said.
Metals made some steady gains on the London Metal Exchange, with copper and aluminium shining.
Three-months copper charged higher, fuelled by widespread buying, to peak at $2,415 per tonne in the afternoon before ending the session at $2,409, a gain of $19.
"Everything's looking very positive," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff.
Many in the market were emboldened after funds showed confidence by borrowing to roll over large positions last week, Adams said.
A fall of 1,750 tonnes in LME-supervised copper stocks, the first in about a week, lent support, while the weaker dollar sparked interest in non-dollar markets.
Aluminium skated to a high of $1,679, but forward selling pushed it back to $1,670 by the close, an $8 gain.
"We will see continued producer forward selling into the strength, but the fundamentals are looking quite good," he said.
The other metals were left behind and strayed little from recent ranges.
Elsewhere in the commodity markets, gold hovered around the $350 an ounce threshold, last seen a month ago, and prices for platinum and palladium also made healthy advances.

Gold was fixed on Monday afternoon in London unchanged from the morning at $348.20 an ounce. But gains in New York Comex gold futures later gave the market another kick to challenge $350, with gains totalling $7.50 from Friday.
The fall in the dollar against the yen to a four-year low of 118 helped shift interest from currencies into gold.
Platinum was indicated at $398.05/$399.05 an ounce, its highest since February 28 and $12.05 up on the day. Palladium set a fresh two-year high of $175.65, up $10.15.
Both rose after a knee jerk downward reaction to a news that a Russian official had said a decree allowing resumed shipments to key importer Japan had been signed and keen interest from funds.

Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade market fell by more than 10 cents to just above $4 per bushel on options-related selling. This exacerbated an early slide triggered by a U.S. Department of Agriculture estimate of U.S. wheat stocks at the end of the 1996-97 year.
It put the number at 465 million bushels, against expectations of 450 million.
"They increased the wheat ending stocks which tells us we're going to have lower wheat prices this year," one trader said.
